Unraveling the Mechanism of Alkali Metal Fluoride
Post-Treatment of SnO2 for Eﬃcient Planar Perovskite Solar
Cells
Minh Tam Hoang, Yang Yang, Wei Hsun Chiu, Yongyue Yu, Ngoc Duy Pham,
Paul Moonie, Andrew Koplick, Gavin Tulloch, Wayde Martens, and Hongxia Wang*
The facile synthesis and beneﬁcial properties of tin oxide have driven the
development of eﬃcient planar perovskite solar cells (PSCs). To increase the
PSC performance, alkali salts are used to treat the SnO2 surface to minimize
the defect states. However, the underlying mechanism of alkali cations’ role in
the PSCs needs further exploration. Herein the eﬀect of alkali ﬂuoride salts
(KF, RbF, and CsF) on the properties of SnO2 and PSC performance is
investigated. The results show diﬀerent alkali have signiﬁcant roles depending
on their nature. Larger cations Cs+ preferably locate at the SnO2 ﬁlm surface
to passivate surface defects and enhance conductivity, while smaller cations
like Rb+ or K+ cations tend to diﬀuse into the perovskite layer to reduce trap
density of the material. The former eﬀect leads to enhanced ﬁll factor while
the latter eﬀect increases the open circuit voltage of the device. It is then
demonstrated that a dual cation post-treatment of the SnO2 layer with RbF
and CsF achieves PSC with a signiﬁcantly higher power conversion eﬃciency
(PCE) of 21.66% compared to pristine PSC with a PCE of 19.71%. This
highlights the signiﬁcance of defect engineering of SnO2 using selective
multiple alkali treatment to improve PSC performance.

1. Introduction
Perovskite solar cell (PSC) is consid-
ered one of the most promising photo-
voltaic technologies to deliver cheap, sus-
tainable, renewable energy by harness-
ing sunlight. The power conversion ef-
ﬁciency (PCE) of PSCs has rapidly been
boosted up to over 25% thanks to the ex-
cellent optical, electrical properties of the
metal halide perovskite materials and the
advancement in material and device engi-
neering in the area of PSCs.[1–3] In a regu-
lar conﬁguration of PSCs, the perovskite
layer is sandwiched between an electron
transport layer (ETL) and a hole trans-
port layer (HTL), thus eﬃcient charge ex-
traction and transportation at the inter-
faces of perovskite/charge extracting lay-
ers are critical to achieve high PCE of
PSCs.[4] Especially the p-type characteris-
tic of perovskite material makes the role
of electron extraction material (n-type)
indispensable.[5] SnO2 is one of the most widely used ETL mate-
rials in PSC because of its suitable band energy alignment with
perovskites, excellent optical transparency, high electron mobility
and excellent chemical and UV stability.[6] Nevertheless, the PCE
of PSC is still limited by nonradiative recombination at the in-
terfacial contact between SnO2 and perovskite layer.[7] Generally,
there are two types of defects on the surface of SnO2 ﬁlm: 1) sur-
face hydroxyl groups and 2) unsaturated Sn dangling bonds or
oxygen vacancies, both can trap electrons and cause detrimen-
tal recombination and degradation.[7,8] Many researches have
demonstrated the importance to passivate these nonradiative de-
fects to facilitate the electron extraction at ETL/perovskite inter-
face, thus promoting the PCE of PSCs.[9]

rionic compounds can react chemically and form bonds with
the hydroxyl groups on the SnO2, thus reducing defects and en-
hancing the charge transport from the perovskite layer, which
in turn leads to PSCs with higher eﬃciency and stability.[10]

can eﬀectively passivate both the positive and negative charged
defects through strong hydrogen bonding and electrostatic in-
teraction. Diﬀerent alkali metal salts including LiF, Li2CO3, KI,

trap density and improving electron conductivity of SnO2.[16–24]
The halide ions (e.g., Cl−and F−) can substitute the defect sites
and dope SnO2 to achieve better optical and electrical properties,
thereby improving the performance of corresponding PSCs.[25–27]
It has been reported that certain salt such as RbF, can also in-
corporate into the upper perovskite layer through ion migra-
tion to suppress unwanted ion migration and nonradiative re-
combination. This allows the fabrication of PSC with high eﬃ-
ciency of 23.38%, smaller hysteresis and open circuit voltage (Voc)
deﬁcit (0.347 V).[22] Clearly, engineering the surface of SnO2 and
SnO2/perovskite interface is critical for fabricating eﬃcient and
stable planar PSCs.
Usage of alkali salt treatment of SnO2 for application in per-
ovskite solar cells has been reported to improve the device perfor-
mance, which was attributed to reduced surface defects.[9] Never-
theless, it seems the inﬂuence of diﬀerent alkali cations on char-
acteristic performance parameters diﬀers. For example, potas-
sium salt treatment of SnO2 was reported to signiﬁcantly en-
hance the Voc and ﬁll factor (FF) of the PSCs,[18,19,28] while Ru+
cation treatment on SnO2 for PSCs predominantly beneﬁted Voc
and hysteresis reduction.[22] Interestingly, the use of Cs+ salt led
to more signiﬁcant eﬀect on the short circuit current density (Jsc)
of the devices by aﬀecting the morphology of the perovskite up-
per layer.[21,23,29] Meanwhile, studies showing that K+ or Cs+ salt
treatment on SnO2 did not pose a signiﬁcant eﬀect on the perfor-
mance of the corresponding PSCs were also reported.[15,30] The
inconsistent and even contradictory results on alkali cations ef-
fect on SnO2 for PSCs suggests more study in this important
area is required. This has motivated us to undertake a systematic
study of the eﬀect of diﬀerent alkali ﬂuoride (namely KF, RbF,
and CsF) post-treatment of SnO2 ETL on the properties of the
ETL and on perovskite ﬁlm, which ultimately inﬂuences the de-
vice performance and stability. By revealing the role of individual
alkali cations, our aim is to develop the most eﬀective yet readily
applied treatment method to increase performance and opera-
tional stability of PSCs using SnO2 based ETL.
Our study has revealed that, the alkali ﬂuoride surface treat-
ment has led to passivation of defects at the interface between
SnO2 and perovskite layer, leading to more eﬃcient charge trans-
fer, thus increased PCE of PSCs. However, the mechanistic role
of each of the alkali cations in the PSC is diﬀerent. Speciﬁcally,
depending on the size of the cations, treatment by the larger alkali
cation like Cs+ increases FF of the PSC through improved surface
properties of SnO2 ﬁlm, while smaller cations like Rb+ and K+
diﬀuse into the perovskite layer, leading to a signiﬁcant enhance-
ment in Voc of the PSCs. Inspired by these ﬁndings, we have fur-
ther developed a new dual-cation treatment strategy of SnO2 ﬁlm
using CsF and RbF simultaneously, which is eﬀective in increas-
ing both the eﬃciency and the stability of PSCs. The correspond-
ing PSC demonstrated a much higher PCE of 21.66% compared
to the PCE of pristine PSCs without treatment (19.71%). Under a
prolonged continuous illumination test for 3 h, the PSC based on
Rb-Cs dual-cation treatment of SnO2 ETL demonstrated 86.6%
performance retention, which is much higher than the device
based on pristine SnO2 ETL (performance retention: 65.9%).
2. Result and Discussion
To create a passivation layer of alkali ﬂuoride salt on SnO2 ﬁlm,
aqueous solutions of 10 mm XF (X = Li, Na, K, Rb, or Cs) were
spin-coated on top of premade SnO2 layer, followed by heat treat-
ment to remove water solvent. Scanning electron microscopy
(SEM) measurement shows that KF, RbF, and CsF can uniformly
distribute on the surface of SnO2/ITO substrate to form a smooth
surface (Figure S1, Supporting Information). However, aggrega-
tion of LiF and NaF clusters on the SnO2 surface were observed.
It could be due to the poor crystallization character of LiF from
aqueous solution leading to formation of microcrystallites on the
ﬁlm.[31] In case of NaF, the irregular morphology is likely orig-
inated from the agglomeration of the free nuclei, which have
been often observed in the process of crystallization of NaF.[32,33]
Since the nonuniform and aggregation are not favorable for sub-
sequently deposition of other layer of materials that are needed
in PSC, therefore, LiF and NaF were not considered further for
the post-treatment of SnO2 ﬁlm by the method utilized in this
work.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurement was
used to reveal the surface properties of SnO2 ﬁlm without and
with XF (X is K, Rb, or Cs) treatment. Upon the treatment, there
is a signiﬁcant amount of F on the surface of SnO2 as evidenced
by the F 1s XPS signal aroused in all samples with the XF treat-
ment (Figure S2, Supporting Information). The XPS peaks of al-
kali cations conﬁrm the presence of these cations after treatment
(Figure S3, Supporting Information). In the Sn 3d XPS spec-
trum (Figure 1a), there is a slight shifting of binding energy to
higher energy. The untreated SnO2 ﬁlm shows peaks of binding
energy at 487.80 and 496.21 eV corresponding to Sn 3d5/2 and Sn
3d3/2, while the XPS peaks (3d5/2, Sn 3d3/2) of SnO2 ﬁlms treated
with KF, RbF, and CsF shift to 487.91 and 496.37 eV, 487.9 and
496.32 eV, and 487.88 and 490.30 eV; respectively. The change in
binding energy can be assigned to incorporation of F into SnO2
by forming Sn–F bonding.[25]
We further investigated the O 1s XPS peaks of SnO2 ﬁlm. The
XPS peaks can be deconvoluted into two component peaks cor-
responding to oxygen in Sn–O bonding (OSn) and oxygen in the
hydroxyl OH group (OH) (Figure 1b). In the pristine samples,
the ratio between the peak component OH/OSn is calculated to
be 0.56, which indicates a signiﬁcant amount of –OH group on
the surface of SnO2 layer. As mentioned before, the –OH group
is an unwanted defect in SnO2 surface that can impair the elec-
tron transport through the layers.[34] In contrast, in the samples
treated with alkali salts XF, we found a signiﬁcant reduction in
the amount of –OH group (Figure S4, Supporting Information).
The OH/OSn ratio decreases from 0.56 to 0.34, 0.34, and 0.37 for
the sample treated with KF, RbF and CsF, respectively. The re-
duced content of –OH group could be assigned to the anion ex-
change reaction with ﬂuorine anions.[14] Thus, we conﬁrm that
the XF treatment helps reduce the trap states on the surface of

We have monitored the evolution of performance of the PSC
without encapsulation under a controlled high humidity condi-
tion (relative humidity (RH): 85 ± 1%). All the devices with XF
treatment demonstrated better stability (Figure S8, Supporting
Information) than the reference PSCs using bare SnO2. Under
the high humidity environment, the reference devices can only
maintain ≈41% of its initial PCE after 48 h. While SnO2:KF ex-

still performed well after 3 h of continuous illumination test.

in the PSCs with XF treatment, we have investigated the ideal-
ity factor (𝜂id) of the device. 𝜂id can be extracted by ﬁtting the
plot of Voc of the devices as a function of light intensity based on
the equation of (𝜂id×KB×T)/q (Figure 2e). In the equation, KB is
the Boltzmann constant, T is temperature, and q is the elemental
charge. The results show the 𝜂id of the device is 1.49, 1.43, 1.27,
and 1.30 for pristine, SnO2:KF, SnO2:RbF, and SnO2:CsF de-
vices, respectively. The smaller 𝜂id reﬂects reduced trap induced
recombination. The result demonstrated that the XF treatment
eﬀectively suppresses the nonradiative recombination of SnO2
surface. Among them, the RbF treatment was the most eﬀective.
We have further investigated the recombination process of the
devices by using impedance spectroscopy (IS). The Nyquist plots
of the corresponding PSCs in dark condition (Figure 2f) are ﬁtted
with an equivalent circuit to extract the recombination resistance.
The equivalent circuit contains a series resistance Rs present-
ing for the ohmic contribution of contacts and wires, two capaci-
tive (Cg and Cs) and two corresponding resistive (R3 and R1) ele-
ments. According to the established model, the Cg capacitance as-
sociated with the dielectric response of the perovskite layer while
the Cs capacitance associated with the surface charge accumula-
tion at the interfaces, these capacitive elements kinetically linked
to the resistive elements R3 and R1, respectively.[41] Previous re-
port has shown that the Cs and R1 dominate the impedance re-
sponse in the low frequency region and connected this type of
low-frequency accumulation capacitance to the build-up of an
electronic accumulation zone formed by majority carrier in the
vicinity of the cathode contact.[42] The geometrical capacitance
Cg and resistance R3 raise from the dielectric response of the
light absorbing perovskite layer, they dominate the impedance re-
sponse in the high-frequency part (>1 kHz). The recombination
dynamic of the device in this case have been shown to be closely
related to the dielectric response from both perovskite layer and
interfacial contacts. The higher value of total recombination re-
sistance (R1 + R3) means lower chance of recombination. Details
of the extracted resistances and capacitance are shown in Table
S1, Supporting Information. The total recombination resistance
(Rrec) is determined by the sum of low and high frequency resis-
tance (R3 and R1). The results show the trend of the Rrec evolution
follows the order of SnO2:RbF (517.1 kΩ) > SnO2:CsF (246.3 kΩ)
> SnO2:KF (210.6 kΩ)> > pristine device (134.5 kΩ). Compared
to the pristine device, the remarkably higher recombination resis-
tance of the XF treated devices indicates a signiﬁcant reduction in
the nonradiative recombination. In particular the SnO2:RbF con-
sistently exhibited the highest recombination resistance. It is also
noticeable that the series resistance of the PSCs also decreased
with the XF treatment. The SnO2:CsF has the lowest Rs (Rs =
13.0 Ω), followed by SnO2:RbF (Rs = 15.5 Ω) < SnO2:KF (Rs =
16.0 Ω) and then pristine PSCs (Rs = 23.1 Ω), the trend is quite
consistent with our conductivity measurements above. The lower
series resistance favors more eﬃcient charge transportation and
collection.

would prominently improve the FF of a PSC,[51] therefore we be-

increase of FF of the corresponding PSCs as observed in Figure

Motivated by the distinguishable beneﬁcial eﬀect of the dif-
ferent alkali cation on the performance of PSCs, we developed
a dual-cation treatment of SnO2 layer by employing RbF and CsF

the recombination in the bulk of the perovskite, which can also
simultaneously inhibit the detrimental ion migration in the bulk
perovskite.[22,52]

As can be seen in Figure S16, Supporting Information, the PSC
with dual cation treatment shows a stable SPO of 20.8%, while
the SPO of pristine device reaches merely to 18.9%. Further-

ment delivered remarkably higher stability with 86.6% of PCE
retention after 3 h operation at maximum power point in air
(RH:30–35%) compared to the device with pristine SnO2 (per-
formance retention rate: 65.9%). Again, we have noticed that the
temperature of both devices went up to 67 °C due to the heat re-
leased by the Xe lamp of the solar simulator. The devices with
dual-cation treatment also exhibited prolonged lifetime under
ambient storage condition (Humidity: 55–65%). After 12 days
of stability test, the PSCs with dual cation treatment retained
68.6% of initial performance while the reference device using
bare SnO2 only shows 54.4% of performance retention (Figure
S17, Supporting Information). The improvement in stability of
device is believed to be related to the signiﬁcant reduction in both
interfacial and bulk defects of the perovskite layers in the pres-
ence of the Cs and Rb cations, which can suppress penetration of
harmful environmental factors such as O2 and H2O into the per-
ovskite while mitigating the detrimental ion migration of halides
or metal cations in the perovskite.[53]
3. Conclusion
In this work, we have revealed the mechanistic role of a series of
alkali cations that was deposited on SnO2 ETL layer in PSCs. The
results have shown that treatment of SnO2 with KF, RbF, and CsF
can improve the electrical properties of SnO2, reduce defect den-
sity as well as enhance charge transportation in PSCs. The role of
alkali cation depends on the nature of the cations. In particular,
the smaller cation like Rb+ and K+ cation can migrate into the up-
per perovskite layer, which subsequently helps reduce defects and
thus recombination in the perovskite layer. This in turn leads to
a much-enhanced Voc of the corresponding. In contrast, the Cs+
tends to remain on the SnO2 ﬁlm to boost the electrical conduc-
tivity of the ETL, and to create better energy band alignment with
the adjacent perovskite layer in the device, which mainly bene-
ﬁts ﬁll factor of the device. Finally, we demonstrate that a Cs-Rb
dual cation treatment strategy of the SnO2 to achieve optimized
interfacial charge transfer and charge transport simultaneously,
leading to superior PCE of 21.66%.
